lead: In CMOS, the source diffusions, the well and the substrate form a hidden four-layer p-n-p-n switch. A current spike can forward-bias one of its junctions. If the parasitic npn and pnp transistors have enough gain and the well and substrate resistances are large enough, they feed each other and the supply rails short together. This is latch-up, and it can destroy or reset a chip. Layout prevents it with frequent substrate and well taps, guard rings, and process choices that lower the parasitic resistances. The current-injection test measures the margin.
prereq: You need the chapter on p-well, n-well and twin-tub processes on well structure and the chapter on layout design rules on layout design rules, because taps and guard rings are spacing decisions as much as circuit decisions.

blocks.text: In an n-well CMOS process, every PMOS sits inside an n-well and every NMOS sits in the p-substrate. The PMOS source is a p+ diffusion tied to VDD. The NMOS source is an n+ diffusion tied to VSS. Between them lie the n-well and the p-substrate. These four regions form a p+ / n-well / p-substrate / n+ stack, which is a p-n-p-n structure.

Two parasitic bipolar transistors appear inside that stack. The pnp transistor has its emitter at the p+ PMOS source (VDD), its base in the n-well, and its collector in the p-substrate. The npn transistor has its emitter at the n+ NMOS source (VSS), its base in the p-substrate, and its collector in the n-well. Neither transistor is drawn or intended, but both are physically present.

The collector of each transistor drives the base of the other. The npn collector is the n-well, which is the pnp base. The pnp collector is the p-substrate, which is the npn base. The n-well has resistance R<sub>well</sub> from the base region to the well tap. The p-substrate has resistance R<sub>sub</sub> from the base region to the substrate tap. Together the two transistors and these two resistors close a positive-feedback loop, as the figure shows.

Latch-up needs a trigger. A current spike on an input or output pad can inject carriers into the substrate. An input undershoot below VSS can forward-bias an n+ diffusion. A fast supply ramp or radiation can create electron-hole pairs. Any of these can make a base-emitter junction conduct. A 2 mA spike through 500 Ω, for example, gives 1.0 V, enough to turn on a silicon junction.
Vsub = Isub × Rsub, Vwell = IC,npn × Rwell, βnpn × βpnp > 1

V<sub>sub</sub> is how far the substrate rises above VSS and V<sub>well</sub> is how far the well falls below VDD (V). I<sub>sub</sub> is the injected substrate current (A). I<sub>C,npn</sub> is the npn collector current flowing from the well tap through R<sub>well</sub> (A). R<sub>sub</sub> and R<sub>well</sub> are the substrate and well resistances (Ω). β<sub>npn</sub> and β<sub>pnp</sub> are the common-emitter current gains of the parasitic transistors. V<sub>sub</sub> raises the substrate above VSS and V<sub>well</sub> lowers the well below VDD; either junction reaching about 0.7 V forward-biases its emitter and turns that transistor on. The loop is regenerative when both emitters are forward biased and the gain product exceeds one.

Both emitters must be forward biased for the loop to close. Once they are on, the npn collector current supplies the pnp base, and the pnp collector current supplies the npn base. If β<sub>npn</sub> × β<sub>pnp</sub> > 1, each pass around the loop adds current. The current rises until the supply limits it. The path then stays on after the trigger is gone, and only removing power resets it. If the gain product is below one, the disturbance dies out.

sections.h3: Prevention: taps, guard rings and process

blocks.text: Layout is the first defence. Place p+ substrate taps tied to VSS close to every NMOS, and n+ well taps tied to VDD close to every PMOS. Tap spacing matters more than tap presence, because R<sub>sub</sub> and R<sub>well</sub> are the resistances from the injection point to the nearest tap. A tap that is far away does little for a device that injects current locally. Put taps on both sides of a wide transistor. Surround sensitive NMOS devices with a p+ guard ring tied to VSS, and sensitive PMOS devices with an n+ guard ring tied to VDD. The ring lowers local resistance and diverts carriers before they reach a parasitic base.

Process choices lower the resistances further. A low-resistance p+ substrate with a thin p-epitaxial layer shunts substrate current. A retrograde well is made by a high-energy implant whose doping peak lies deep, near the bottom of the well, while the surface stays lightly doped. The heavy buried layer lowers the well resistance R<sub>well</sub> and raises the doping of the vertical pnp base, which cuts β<sub>pnp</sub>. Shallow trench isolation removes the deep sidewall paths of older LOCOS isolation. Silicide on diffusions and taps reduces sheet resistance. A standard current-injection latch-up test injects current into a pin, removes it, and checks whether the supply current stays high; a sustained high current means the chip has latched.

examples.question: An n-well CMOS inverter has R<sub>sub</sub> = 200 Ω and R<sub>well</sub> = 1 kΩ, with β<sub>npn</sub> = 50 and β<sub>pnp</sub> = 20. A spike injects 2 mA into the substrate. (a) Find the substrate drop; the npn emitter needs 0.7 V to turn on. Does it turn on? (b) Repeat for R<sub>sub</sub> = 500 Ω. (c) Given that both emitters are forward biased, is the loop regenerative?
steps: Convert the injected current: I<sub>inj</sub> = 2 mA = 0.002 A.
For R<sub>sub</sub> = 200 Ω, V<sub>sub</sub> = I<sub>inj</sub> × R<sub>sub</sub> = 0.002 A × 200 Ω = 0.4 V. Since 0.4 V < 0.7 V, the npn does not turn on.
For R<sub>sub</sub> = 500 Ω, V<sub>sub</sub> = I<sub>inj</sub> × R<sub>sub</sub> = 0.002 A × 500 Ω = 1.0 V. Since 1.0 V > 0.7 V, the npn turns on.
The loop gain is β<sub>npn</sub> × β<sub>pnp</sub> = 50 × 20 = 1000. Since 1000 > 1, once both emitters are forward biased each pass around the loop adds current, so the loop is regenerative.
examples.answer: With R<sub>sub</sub> = 200 Ω the substrate drop is 0.4 V, below 0.7 V, so the npn stays off and there is no latch-up; with R<sub>sub</sub> = 500 Ω the drop is 1.0 V and the npn turns on. Given that both emitters are forward biased, yes, the loop is regenerative, because β<sub>npn</sub> × β<sub>pnp</sub> = 1000 > 1 and each pass around the loop adds current.

V1 = I * R_sub1

R_sub2 = 500
V2 = I * R_sub2
beta = 50 * 20
print(V1)

examples.question: An n-well is 20 μm wide with sheet resistance 1 kΩ per square. A pad can inject up to 0.2 mA into the well, and the well drop must stay below 0.3 V so the pnp emitter-base junction stays off with margin. How far from the injection point may the nearest well tap be?
steps: Largest allowed well resistance: R<sub>well</sub> = V/I = 0.3 V ÷ 0.2×10⁻³ A = 1500 Ω.
One square of a 20 μm wide well is 20 μm long, so the path may be 1.5 × 20 μm = 30 μm long.
examples.answer: The nearest n<sup>+</sup> well tap must be within 30 μm of the injection point; taps every 30 μm or closer along the well meet the limit.

traps: Adding a tap anywhere is not enough: what matters is the resistance from the injection point to the nearest tap. A distant tap leaves a large R<sub>sub</sub> or R<sub>well</sub>.
Latch-up is not the same as ESD damage. ESD is a fast overvoltage event; latch-up is a sustained low-resistance path that remains after the trigger.
The loop condition is the product β<sub>npn</sub> × β<sub>pnp</sub> > 1, not the sum. One weak device does not make the loop safe: β<sub>npn</sub> = 5 with β<sub>pnp</sub> = 0.5 still gives 2.5 > 1.
A tap does not replace a guard ring. The ring lowers local resistance and diverts carriers, while the tap sets the reference potential.
In the current-injection test, the chip has latched only if the supply current stays high after the injected current is removed; a temporary rise is not latch-up.

quiz.q: Name the four layers of the parasitic p-n-p-n path in an n-well process.
quiz.a: p+ PMOS source, n-well, p-substrate, n+ NMOS source.

quiz.q: Why does a larger R<sub>sub</sub> make latch-up easier?
quiz.a: A given injected current produces a larger I × R<sub>sub</sub> drop, so the npn base-emitter junction reaches 0.7 V sooner.

quiz.q: R<sub>sub</sub> = 300 Ω, I<sub>inj</sub> = 2 mA, V<sub>BE</sub>(on) = 0.7 V. Does the npn turn on?
A layout has taps only at the far edge of a large n-well. Explain the latch-up risk.
quiz.a: The n-well resistance from the PMOS to the tap remains large. Injected current causes a bigger well drop, forward-biasing the pnp and closing the loop.

quiz.q: β<sub>npn</sub> = 40 and β<sub>pnp</sub> = 30. Is the loop gain regenerative?
What does a p+ guard ring around an NMOS tied to VSS do?
quiz.a: It places a low-resistance p+ contact close to the NMOS, reducing R<sub>sub</sub> and diverting carriers before they reach the npn base region.

quiz.q: Why can a thin p-epitaxial layer on a p+ substrate reduce latch-up?
quiz.a: The p+ substrate is a low-resistance path to the substrate tap. The thin epitaxial layer limits the volume and resistance of the p region, so R<sub>sub</sub> falls and the pnp collector current is shunted.

quiz.q: What does the current-injection latch-up test observe?
quiz.a: It injects current into a pin and monitors supply current; latch-up is a sustained high supply current after the injected current is removed.

beyond: Not for the exam. In advanced nodes, latch-up margin is built from epitaxial substrates, retrograde wells, trench isolation, and dense tap patterns rather than from one magic rule. I/O circuits receive extra guard rings because they see the outside world. The current-injection test remains the language used in datasheets and qualification reports. Search next for 'latch-up current injection test', 'guard ring layout', and 'retrograde well latch-up'.
